title: Determinants of health, inequalities and epidemiology
blurb: Explain what shapes health beyond healthcare, how inequalities are tackled, and read incidence and prevalence correctly.
question: Mr Bianchi, 72, has COPD and has been admitted three times since November. He lives alone in a rented flat with black mould, keeps the heating off to save money and finds reading difficult. Which factors in his life are wider determinants of health, and how should the nurse adapt her information for him?

teach.h: Health is made mostly outside the clinic
teach.body: The determinants of health are the conditions that shape how healthy people are: biology, behaviour, relationships, housing, work, income and the wider economy and culture. Health inequalities are unfair, avoidable differences in health between groups. In plain English: where you are born, live, work and age shapes your health long before you meet a nurse.

teach.topLabel: Outer layers: furthest from individual control
teach.caption: Living and working conditions include education, work, unemployment, water and sanitation, health services, housing and food. Layers interact.

teach.h: The social gradient and proportionate universalism
teach.body: The Marmot Review, Fair Society, Healthy Lives (February 2010), showed a social gradient: health gets better step by step with each rung up the social ladder, not just between rich and poor. Its answer was proportionate universalism: actions should be universal, but with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage. Its six objectives begin with 'give every child the best start in life'.
teach.cite: Marmot Review 2010, Institute of Health Equity

items.label: male life expectancy gap, least vs most deprived

teach.caption: Public Health England, Health matters: life course approach (2019). The gap in years lived in good health is about twice the gap in lifespan.

head: Part
Meaning
rows: Locally identified groups, e.g. inclusion health
Maternity; severe mental illness; chronic respiratory disease; early cancer diagnosis; hypertension and lipids
teach.caption: PLUS groups expected include ethnic minority communities, people with a learning disability and autistic people, and people with multiple long-term conditions. Early cancer ambition: 75% diagnosed at stage 1 or 2 by 2028.

teach.body: Health literacy is a person's ability to understand and use information to make decisions about their health, and also a 'systems issue' about how complex information and services are. NHS England cites evidence that up to 61% of England's working-age population do not routinely understand the health information they are given, with a strong social gradient. Use plain language, pictures, 'chunk and check', and teach-back: ask the person to explain in their own words.

teach.caption: A long-lasting disease with low incidence can still have high prevalence, because cases build up (HealthKnowledge).

teach.body: Worldwide, noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) killed at least 43 million people in 2021, 75% of non-pandemic deaths; 73% of NCD deaths are in low- and middle-income countries. The main groups are cardiovascular disease, cancers, chronic respiratory disease and diabetes. The four main behavioural risk factors are tobacco, unhealthy diet, harmful use of alcohol and physical inactivity.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Bianchi on the respiratory ward
teach.body: Staff nurse Amara sees that Mr Bianchi's COPD is worsened by things outside the hospital: a cold, damp flat (living conditions), low income (socio-economic), and living alone (social networks). She refers him for a benefits and housing assessment through the discharge team. Knowing he finds reading hard, she teaches inhaler use with a picture leaflet, in small chunks, and asks him to show and tell her back what he will do. He lives in a Core20 area, so the local COPD service prioritises his follow-up.

teach.text: Don't mix up incidence and prevalence. 'How many NEW cases this year?' is incidence. 'How many people HAVE the condition now?' is prevalence. And the Core20 is the most deprived 20% of the population by the Index of Multiple Deprivation, not the 20% with the worst health.

items: Rainbow model layers: fixed core, lifestyle, social networks, living and working conditions, wider socio-economic conditions.
Marmot 2010: social gradient; proportionate universalism; give every child the best start.
Core20PLUS5: most deprived 20% (IMD), local PLUS groups, five clinical areas.
Health literacy: up to 61% of working-age adults struggle; use teach-back, chunk and check.
Incidence = new cases over time; prevalence = existing cases at a point or period.
Global: NCDs cause 75% of non-pandemic deaths; four main risk factors.

summary: You can now place a person's circumstances within the layers of the determinants of health and explain the social gradient and proportionate universalism. You can also apply Core20PLUS5, adapt information for health literacy and tell incidence from prevalence.

A.q: A practice nurse reads that 240 adults in a town of 80,000 were newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes last year. Which measure does this describe?
A.why: New cases over a defined period in a population at risk is incidence.

whyNot.0: Prevalence counts all existing cases, not just new ones.
whyNot.3: Life expectancy is the average expected lifespan, not a count of cases.

A.q: In NHS England's Core20PLUS5 approach for adults, what does 'Core20' refer to?
options: The 20% of patients with the most long-term conditions
The 20 clinical conditions with the widest outcome gaps
The 20% of GP practices with the longest waiting lists
The most deprived 20% of the national population by IMD
A.why: Core20 is the most deprived 20% of the national population as identified by the national Index of Multiple Deprivation (NHS England).

whyNot.0: People with multiple long-term conditions are an expected PLUS group, not the Core20.
whyNot.1: The '5' refers to five clinical areas, and there is no list of 20 conditions.
whyNot.2: Core20 describes a population, not a set of practices.

A.q: In the Dahlgren and Whitehead model, which layer does damp, overcrowded housing belong to?
A.why: Housing sits in the living and working conditions layer, alongside education, work, water and sanitation, and health services.

whyNot.1: Lifestyle factors are behaviours such as smoking and diet.
whyNot.2: Social networks are relationships with family, friends and community.
whyNot.3: The core is fixed biological factors.

B.q: On 1 April, 900 of a practice's 15,000 adults have diagnosed asthma. Which measure is this?
B.why: All existing cases at a single point in time is point prevalence.

whyNot.1: Cumulative incidence counts new cases over a period, not all existing cases.
whyNot.2: An attack rate is the proportion who become ill during an outbreak.
whyNot.3: Case fatality is the proportion of cases who die from the disease.

B.q: Mrs Doyle, 66, is starting a new insulin pen at home. She tells the community nurse she 'never got on with forms and booklets'. After demonstrating the pen, what is the best way to check her understanding?
options: Ask her if she has any questions
Give her the manufacturer's leaflet to read later
Ask her to show and tell you how she will use it
Ask her whether she understood the explanation
B.why: Teach-back asks the person to explain or demonstrate in their own words, which checks real understanding (NHS England health literacy).

whyNot.0: Many people with low health literacy will not ask questions, so this does not check understanding.
whyNot.1: A dense leaflet does not suit someone who struggles with written information.
whyNot.3: A yes/no question invites 'yes' without confirming understanding.

B.q: A health board offers a home visiting programme to all new families, with extra visits for families in the most deprived areas. Which principle does this illustrate?
B.why: Marmot (2010): actions should be universal, but with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage.

whyNot.0: Rose's prevention paradox is about population measures benefiting each individual little.
whyNot.1: The inverse care law describes good care being least available where it is most needed, the problem rather than this solution.
whyNot.2: A high-risk approach would offer the programme to the high-risk families alone.

C.q: A nurse compares two areas. In the least deprived, men live about 9 years longer than in the most deprived. The healthy life expectancy gap is about 19 years. What does this mainly show?
options: Men in deprived areas live longer but in poorer health
Healthy life expectancy is unaffected by deprivation
They die sooner and spend more years unwell
Life expectancy and healthy life expectancy are the same
C.why: PHE (2019): the healthy life expectancy gap (19.1 years for men) is about double the life expectancy gap (9.4 years), so people in deprived areas die sooner and spend more of their lives in poor health.

whyNot.0: Men in the most deprived areas live about 9 years less, not longer; only the years in poor health are greater.
whyNot.1: The large healthy life expectancy gap shows deprivation strongly affects it.
whyNot.3: The two measures differ; healthy life expectancy counts years in good health.

C.q: Which of the following is one of the five clinical areas in the adult Core20PLUS5 approach?
C.why: The five adult areas are maternity, severe mental illness, chronic respiratory disease, early cancer diagnosis, and hypertension case-finding with optimal lipid management.

whyNot.1: Dementia diagnosis is not one of the five adult clinical areas.
whyNot.2: Childhood obesity relates to the separate children and young people's version, not the adult five.
whyNot.3: Hip fracture care is not one of the five areas.

C.q: Globally, which group of conditions does the WHO identify as causing most deaths from noncommunicable diseases?
C.why: WHO (2025): cardiovascular diseases account for most NCD deaths (at least 19 million in 2021), followed by cancers, chronic respiratory diseases and diabetes.

whyNot.0: Cancers are second, at about 10 million deaths.
whyNot.2: Chronic respiratory diseases caused about 4 million deaths.
whyNot.3: Diabetes caused over 2 million deaths, fewer than the others listed.

reteach.title: Peel the onion
reteach.question: If you peeled back the layers of a person's life, which layers would you find shaping their health?

blocks.body: At the centre are things the person cannot change: age, sex and genes. Next come their behaviours: smoking, diet, activity. Around those are their relationships and community. Then their daily conditions: housing, work, education, access to services. On the outside: the economy, culture and environment of the whole country. The further out, the less control the individual has, and the more policy and services matter.

blocks.text: Prevalence is like a bath: incidence is the tap filling it, and recovery or death is the plug draining it.

explain.body: Dahlgren and Whitehead (1991): fixed core of age, sex and hereditary factors, then individual lifestyle factors, social and community networks, living and working conditions, and general socio-economic, cultural and environmental conditions.

test.q: Which is a fixed factor at the core of the Dahlgren and Whitehead model?
test.why: The core contains fixed factors: age, sex and hereditary factors.

whyNot.0: Smoking is an individual lifestyle factor.
whyNot.1: Unemployment is in living and working conditions.
whyNot.2: Housing is in living and working conditions.

explain.body: Fair Society, Healthy Lives (2010): the social gradient; proportionate universalism; six objectives starting with giving every child the best start in life.

explain.caption: Illustrative: health improves step by step up the social ladder.

test.q: What is the first of the six Marmot Review policy objectives?
options: Give every child the best start in life
Create fair employment and good work for all
Ensure a healthy standard of living for all
test.why: Marmot (2010) objective 1: give every child the best start in life.

explain.body: Ability to understand and use health information, plus how complex the system is. Up to 61% of working-age adults in England do not routinely understand health information. Use plain words, pictures, chunk and check, and teach-back.

test.q: According to evidence cited by NHS England, up to what proportion of working-age adults in England do not routinely understand health information they are given?
test.why: NHS England health literacy page: up to 61% of the English working-age population.

whyNot.1: 31% is about half the cited figure.

explain.body: Incidence: new cases in a population at risk over a period. Prevalence: all existing cases at a point (point prevalence) or over a period. Chronic diseases have prevalence much higher than incidence.

test.q: A cure is introduced for a chronic disease, but the number of new cases each year stays the same. What will happen to prevalence over time?
test.why: Prevalence depends on new cases and how long people have the disease. A cure shortens duration, so fewer people have the disease at any time.

whyNot.0: Prevalence rises when duration increases, for example when survival improves without cure.
whyNot.2: Shorter duration with unchanged incidence lowers prevalence.
whyNot.3: Prevalence falls gradually; it does not instantly equal incidence.
